name: Bit Manipulation
description: Use bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, shifts) to solve problems in O(1) extra space or O(n) time where a naive approach would need extra memory or comparisons - especially common for single-number/duplicate-detection and subset-enumeration problems.
core_technique: Lean on core identities: XOR of a number with itself is 0 and with 0 is itself (so XOR-ing a list cancels out pairs, leaving the odd one out); `n & (n-1)` clears the lowest set bit (useful for counting set bits or checking powers of two); a bitmask from 0 to 2^n - 1 can represent every possible subset of an n-element set, where bit i being 1 means element i is included.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting XOR is both commutative and associative, which is WHY order doesn't matter when cancelling pairs - not realizing this can lead to overcomplicating a one-line solution; sign/overflow issues when shifting in languages with fixed-width integers (less of a concern in Python, but worth mentioning if the problem is language-agnostic); using bit tricks for readability's sake when a simple hashmap/set solution is clearer and the interviewer didn't ask for the O(1)-space optimization.

example_problems.title: Single Number
example_problems.why_it_fits: Every element appears twice except one - XOR-ing the entire array cancels all pairs (a^a=0), leaving only the unpaired element, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

example_problems.title: Number of 1 Bits
example_problems.why_it_fits: Repeatedly apply `n & (n-1)` to clear the lowest set bit and count how many times you can do this before n becomes 0 - faster than checking each of 32 bits individually.

example_problems.title: Subsets
example_problems.why_it_fits: Alternative to the backtracking approach - iterate bitmasks from 0 to 2^n - 1, and for each, check which bits are set to determine which elements are included in that subset.

additional_considerations: When a bit trick feels like the 'clever' answer, also be ready to explain the straightforward hashmap/set approach first - interviewers often want to see you recognize the space/time tradeoff being made, not just recite the trick. For subset-via-bitmask problems, explicitly connect it back to the Backtracking pattern as an alternative approach to the same problem - showing you see the two are solving the same underlying question differently is a strong signal.
